name: Cross-tradition comparisons
summary: Cross-tradition comparison concepts and CONTRASTS_WITH / SIMILAR_TO links between concepts in the six tradition files. Every comparison restates claims already in those files and cites their sources, re-declared here as "<tradition>:<id>". No new facts are added. Each comparison concept lists the concepts it compares in a "compares" array.

sources.title: Profile: Bagru Textiles' Indian Blockprints
sources.author: The Kind Craft (unsigned)
sources.notes: Blog profile of the Bagru Textiles enterprise, published 3 April 2017, unsigned; the page does not describe its interview basis: block terms gudh/rekh/datta, block woods, motif names (leher, chaupad, kangura, jaali), dabu recipe, syahi/begar ingredients, seasonality and falling water table. sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

sources.title: Dabu printing Akola | Story of Indian crafts and craftsmen
sources.author: Gaatha (unattributed)
sources.notes: Craft-organisation field documentation of Akola: legend, Chhipa community, Beduch river settlement, mud+gum+lime paste, indigo, alizarin->naphthol, tar substitution, motifs (Kahma, Lal titri, Dholika, Kantedar), Phetiya garments, Kishangarh fabric, Udaipur pigments.

sources.title: Block Print~Akola (Craft Archive)
sources.author: Gaatha (unattributed)
sources.notes: Detailed cluster documentation of Akola: location (Bhopalsagar tehsil, Chittorgarh), ~200 practitioners, allied communities, 14 traditional block designs, current tar/oil/rogan resist replacing mud (mud cracked), naphthol + red salt reds, ash dusting, indigo cold bath green->blue, boiling to remove tar, tools, challenges (fumes, water use, groundwater pollution). Intro inconsistently names Udaipur district. Fact-check 2026-10-14: page also explains naphthol/diazo salt coupling and records the zigzag phetiya border and kadhai-like boilers.

sources.title: Block printing the impermeable clay Dabu
sources.author: Craft Revival Trust
sources.publisher: Craft Revival Trust Archive via Google Arts & Culture
sources.notes: Documented at Deesa, Gujarat (not Akola). Paste of river-bed silt, local gum, lime, sugarcane molasses and water; kneaded by stamping over several days; strained; sawdust over wet paste; sun-dried until hard; dip-dyed; repeated per colour.

sources.title: GI Application No. 845 - Aakola Dabu Prints
sources.author: Geographical Indications Registry
sources.notes: Applicant Udhyam Protsahan Sansthan; filed 04-03-2022; Class 24 handicrafts; status Pre Examination (not registered) as of access date. Statement of Case listed but not read.

sources.title: Hand Block Printing of Akola, Rajasthan
sources.author: Global InCH (unattributed)
sources.publisher: Global InCH - International Journal of Living Heritage
sources.notes: Akola dabu types phetia and nangna; three resists of increasing strength: chuna/lime (kirana), mitti/mud, rait/sand; also describes a boiled bedja-gum + oil hot resist with ash dusting, metal blocks, naphthol/alizarin. Places Akola in Udaipur district. Fact-check: Phetia worn by Jat and Chaudhury women after childbirth or at weddings; nangna by Gujjar women (occasion not given).

sources.title: Indigo Dye Workshop
sources.author: Pratt's Textile Dye Garden
sources.notes: Clay resist works only with indigo because vat is cold and immersion brief; most natural dyes need heat and long immersion which would wash clay off; indigo turns green to blue as it oxygenates.

sources.title: Dabu Printing
sources.author: Rao, Bindu Gopal
sources.publisher: bindugopalrao.com (first published in Apparel magazine, April 2019)
sources.notes: Journalist interview with an Akola printer: clay, chuna, wheat chaff, gum from acacia/babul; mud dug from a dry pond and soaked overnight; sawdust; hot-sun drying; repeat cycles; uneven cracks and veining; challenges. Fact-check: article spells the word "Dabana"; dated 3 May 2019 on the blog.

sources.title: Craft Name: Dabu (Craft Katha)
sources.author: All India Artisans and Craftworkers Welfare Association (AIACA)
sources.notes: Black clay, lime and natural gum; "fermented mud paste"; light crackle effect; 5-15 days and 2-4 artisans per piece; attributes craft to Khatri community; claims GI tag in 2023 (contradicted by S5). Fact-check: page says "Khatris" and lists "Light crackle effect visible in resist areas" as an authenticity marker; no publication date (footer 2025).

sources.title: 'Bagru' - A Traditional Printing Technique of Rajasthan
sources.author: Raj, Sambaditya
sources.notes: Added by fact-check. Bagru-centred (not Akola). Scouring with a paste of cow dung, soda ash and sesame oil ("Hari sarana"); harda (myrobalan) wash whose tannic acid acts as mordant for the iron of the black (syahi); dabu = lime, "Bedhan" (worm-spoiled wheat flour) and black clay, mashed, left overnight, strained; Kaligar/Dolidar/Gawarbali dabu types; sawdust; indigo then pomegranate, then alum-water rinse to fix colour, alum quantity varying with dabu strength. Year from PDF metadata (2012); no peer review.

sources.title: Kalamkari — The Block Prints of Machalipatnam (craft documentation)
sources.author: Craftmark (All India Artisans and Craftworkers Welfare Association) — individual author not stated
sources.notes: Most detailed process source: producer communities, raw materials, tools with dimensions, 11 production stages, preparation of kasim (iron acetate) and karam (alum), myrobalan, alizarin boiling with jajaku leaves, colour recipes, second printing, alum fixing, soaping. Undated (prices quoted as of Aug 2004); cites Varadarajan (NID 1982) and Census of India AP crafts volume. Fact-check: the 11-stage list in section 6 differs in order from the narrated process (6.a-6.f); the narrated order is the one used for PRECEDES. Captions show background printed with alum and outline/stem-fill with iron acetate.

sources.title: Hand Block-Printing / Kalamkari of Machilipatnam, Andhra Pradesh
sources.author: Asia InCH (Encyclopedia of Intangible Cultural Heritage)
sources.publisher: Asia InCH - Encyclopedia of Intangible Cultural Heritage (Craft Revival Trust)

Fact-check: the wax-resist/indigo/kalam passage is a general kalamkari description, not specific to Machilipatnam block printing.

sources.title: Bed curtain, Coromandel Coast, c.1700 (IS.121-1950)
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
sources.notes: Coromandel chintz technique: alum mordant for red, iron mordant for black; indigo needs no mordant so wax resist used; green = yellow over indigo.

sources.title: Chintz hanging fragments, Coromandel Coast, early 18th century (IM.50-1919 etc.)
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
sources.notes: Chintz = mordant and resist techniques associated with the Coromandel Coast because of local soil, water and dye plants; large imports to Britain and Netherlands in 17th–18th c.

sources.title: Kalamkari: An Introduction
sources.author: Rajarshi Sengupta
sources.notes: Machilipatnam vs Srikalahasti: karkhanas, block makers from carpenter community, teak blocks one per colour, washing at Kalia Canal, iron boiling vessels, gaja leaves; states alum is NOT used for red at Machilipatnam (conflicts with S3/S4). sources.title: As fake Kalamkari takes over the market, the original struggles in Andhra's Pedana

sources.notes: Journalism with artisan testimony: cow-dung soak and pond washing, myrobalan + buffalo milk, copper-vessel boiling, black from iron scrap/jaggery/salt in buried jar 21 days, starch/alum/soap finish; screen-printing competition and canal pollution; states GI 2012. Fact-check: dated 24 Jul 2018; article step order matches Craftmark (scour, myrobalan, print, wash, boil, wash, starch, second colour, alum, soap).

concepts.title: Resist methods: clay pastes, lime outlines and wax
concepts.summary: Ajrakh gach is a paste of tree gum, clay (lal mitti), water and millet flour, with alum added to half of it; the clay and millet resist indigo while the alum acts as mordant.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh gach is a paste of tree gum, clay (lal mitti), water and millet flour, with alum added to half of it; the clay and millet resist indigo while the alum acts as mordant. [ajrakh:S1]

Ajrakh white outlines (khariyanu) are printed with a lime and tree-gum resist. [ajrakh:S1]

Dabu paste is mud, gum and lime; the Deesa paste uses river-bed silt. [dabu:S1, dabu:S3]

In Dabu sources lime is the weakest resist, used for fine outlines, mud is used for repeated indigo immersion and sand for absorbent colours. [dabu:S6]

Bagru and Sanganeri dabu paste mixes black clay (kali mitti), lime, wheat flour and gum in ratios that depend on the type of dabu needed, and is used only for indigo patterns. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Beeswax is listed as a Machilipatnam raw material; wax applied with a kalam before indigo appears in a general kalamkari description. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4, machilipatnam-kalamkari:S5]

claims.text: Ajrakh gach is a paste of tree gum, clay (lal mitti), water and millet flour, with alum added to half of it; the clay and millet resist indigo while the alum acts as mordant.
Ajrakh white outlines (khariyanu) are printed with a lime and tree-gum resist.
Dabu paste is mud, gum and lime; the Deesa paste uses river-bed silt.
In Dabu sources lime is the weakest resist, used for fine outlines, mud is used for repeated indigo immersion and sand for absorbent colours.
Bagru and Sanganeri dabu paste mixes black clay (kali mitti), lime, wheat flour and gum in ratios that depend on the type of dabu needed, and is used only for indigo patterns.
Beeswax is listed as a Machilipatnam raw material; wax applied with a kalam before indigo appears in a general kalamkari description.

concepts.title: Indigo application: resist-and-dip versus direct printing
concepts.summary: Ajrakh cloth is folded and dipped in the indigo vat, turns green then blue in air, and the darkest blues need three or four immersions.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh cloth is folded and dipped in the indigo vat, turns green then blue in air, and the darkest blues need three or four immersions. [ajrakh:S1]

Dabu cloth is dip-dyed in a cold indigo bath after the paste hardens, repeated until the shade is reached. [dabu:S3, dabu:S2]

Bagru and Sanganeri cloth is pleated, opened under the liquor and re-dipped; the first dip gives pale sky blue. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

At Machilipatnam indigo is mixed with rice starch and printed directly because it needs no mordant. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4]

Khatri printers could judge an indigo vat by tasting it; Bagru and Sanganer dyers judge it by its colour. [ajrakh:S8, ajrakh:S11, bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

claims.text: Ajrakh cloth is folded and dipped in the indigo vat, turns green then blue in air, and the darkest blues need three or four immersions.
Dabu cloth is dip-dyed in a cold indigo bath after the paste hardens, repeated until the shade is reached.
Bagru and Sanganeri cloth is pleated, opened under the liquor and re-dipped; the first dip gives pale sky blue.
At Machilipatnam indigo is mixed with rice starch and printed directly because it needs no mordant.
Khatri printers could judge an indigo vat by tasting it; Bagru and Sanganer dyers judge it by its colour.

concepts.title: Mordant systems: myrobalan, alum and iron
concepts.summary: Ajrakh cloth is soaked in harde and dried without rinsing; tannin is an essential pre-mordant aiding adhesion of printed mordants.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh cloth is soaked in harde and dried without rinsing; tannin is an essential pre-mordant aiding adhesion of printed mordants. [ajrakh:S1]

Bagh cloth is dyed in harara and turns yellowish; harara strengthens the tones of the black and red printed later. [bagh:S1]

Bagru and Sanganeri cloth is treated with harda, whose tannic acid attracts the mordants applied by block. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Machilipatnam cloth soaks 30–45 minutes in myrobalan, is squeezed and dried in sunlight. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S3]

Iron black is made from iron fermented with jaggery or molasses: scrap iron in Ajrakh (kut), iron strips with jaggery and salt water in Machilipatnam (kasim), and an iron-molasses-gum solution in Bagru and Sanganeri (syahi); the Bagh GI describes iron sulphate or iron filings with jaggery. [ajrakh:S1, bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1, machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4, bagh:S1]

In Bagru, Sanganeri and Bagh the alizarin bath develops red on alum-printed areas and black on iron-printed areas. In Machilipatnam the black is produced earlier, by iron reacting with the myrobalan tannin, and the alizarin bath helps fix that black. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1, bagh:S7, machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4]

A low-reliability Bagru account is the only Dabu-file source for harda and alum mordanting. [dabu:S23]

concepts.title: Red dye sources and red-bath additives
concepts.summary: Ajrakh uses Indian madder (Rubia cordifolia) or synthetic alizarin, which superseded madder and also requires alum.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh uses Indian madder (Rubia cordifolia) or synthetic alizarin, which superseded madder and also requires alum. [ajrakh:S1]

At Bagh the aal root was earlier used; alizarine has taken its place. [bagh:S1]

Bagru and Sanganeri red baths use madder, now synthetic alizarin due to shortage. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Madder and chay were fine southern red sources; Machilipatnam now uses alizarin brought from Mumbai. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4]

In Akola Dabu, alizarin red was later replaced by naphthol developed in red salt. [dabu:S1, dabu:S2]

Dhawai flowers are boiled with alizarin at Bagru and Sanganer to avoid patches and staining. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Dhavda flowers are used for shine and fixing in the Bagh boiling solution. [bagh:S1]

Ajrakh dyers add dried tamarisk flowers if colour spreads into white areas. [ajrakh:S1]

Machilipatnam dyers add jajaku leaves to the alizarin bath as a carrier that hastens dyeing. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4]

concepts.title: The ground after the red bath: white, cream or pink
concepts.summary: Madder often leaves a pinkish tinge on Ajrakh whites; the cloth is soaked in camel dung and spread on sandy river banks in the sun, sprinkled with water, for at least three days.
concepts.body_md:
Madder often leaves a pinkish tinge on Ajrakh whites; the cloth is soaked in camel dung and spread on sandy river banks in the sun, sprinkled with water, for at least three days. [ajrakh:S1]

Alizarin tints the Sanganeri ground off-white or yellow, so it is laid on a river bed and sprinkled with dilute cow dung as it dries; the GI calls this the most typical Sanganeri step. [sanganeri:S1]

In Bagh tarai the cloth is washed three to four times in the stream and repeatedly moistened while drying. [bagh:S1]

The Bagru ground is mostly off-white (cream), while the Sanganeri background is white. [bagru:S1]

At Machilipatnam, portions not treated with alum imbibe a pinkish colour in the alizarin bath. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4]

concepts.title: Process length and stage counts
concepts.summary: Ajrakh: 15–16 stages over 15–21 days (GI), about 14 stages (V&A label), 16 stages (Mongabay).
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh: 15–16 stages over 15–21 days (GI), about 14 stages (V&A label), 16 stages (Mongabay). [ajrakh:S1, ajrakh:S3, ajrakh:S10]

Ajrakh scouring (saaj) is repeated eight to ten times. [ajrakh:S1]

Each Bagh sari takes at least three weeks after printing, is washed at least three times and goes to the bhatti at least twice. [bagh:S1]

Bagh printed cloth is kept eight to fifteen days so the colour sets. [bagh:S1]

Bagru and Sanganeri printed fabric is left at least three to four days, and longer ageing gives a better result. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Machilipatnam printed cloth is kept two to three days until dry; the whole process takes almost two months. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4]

Dabu resist-and-dye is repeated through a dye bath for each colour. [dabu:S3]

concepts.title: Water and environmental dependence
concepts.summary: Ajrakh printing concentrated where extra soft water was available; iron in the water dulls and darkens the result.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh printing concentrated where extra soft water was available; iron in the water dulls and darkens the result. [ajrakh:S1]

Bagh's proximity to the river was an important reason for its choice; the river water's chemistry is said to give luminous tones. [bagh:S1]

Bagru water is claimed to have excellent properties for dyeing, and the Sanjaria river now runs dry. [bagru:S1, bagru:S4]

The water of the river "Saraswati" is credited with Sanganer's characteristic shades. [sanganeri:S10]

Coromandel chintz pre-eminence is attributed to local soil, water and dye plants. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S11]

Akola depends on the Beduch river plus hand pumps and tube wells; the craft archive calls for water reuse and reports that chemical residues pollute groundwater. [dabu:S2]

Untreated Sanganer printing wastewater pollutes the Amanishah Nallah and groundwater. [sanganeri:S11]

concepts.title: Printer communities: Chhipa and Khatri histories
concepts.summary: Ajrakh came to Kutch from Sindh some 400 years ago when the King of Kutch invited Khatri craftsmen.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh came to Kutch from Sindh some 400 years ago when the King of Kutch invited Khatri craftsmen. [ajrakh:S1]

The Khatri community of chhipas is believed to have come to Bagh about 400 years ago from Larkana in Sindh. [bagh:S1]

Bagru Chhipas migrated from Sawai Madhopur, Alwar, Jhunjhunu and Sikar districts about 300 years ago and claim descent from Saint Namdeo. [bagru:S1, bagru:S5]

The Chhipa printers of Sanganer are described as Hindus who follow Sant Namdev. [sanganeri:S10]

The Akola block printers are the Chippa community. [dabu:S1, dabu:S2]

Survey respondents in Bagru and Sanganer were mostly from the Khatri or Chhipa community. [bagru:S3, sanganeri:S4]

Machilipatnam printing is done in karkhanas; castes named include Devangas, Padmasalis, Kannebhaktulu and Senapathalu, with Hindu and Muslim dyers. [machilipatnam-kalamkari:S4, machilipatnam-kalamkari:S3]

concepts.title: Designs tied to client communities
concepts.summary: Maldhari groups (including Jat) each had distinct Ajrakh styles and palettes that Khatris did not change.
concepts.body_md:
Maldhari groups (including Jat) each had distinct Ajrakh styles and palettes that Khatris did not change. [ajrakh:S7]

Bagh artisans formerly made different prints and clothes for different communities and castes, including Jat; now only Adivasis retain this. [bagh:S1]

Colours and designs of Bagru prints identify the user community (Jat, Meena, Rajput, Mali). [bagru:S1]

The Dabu phetia was worn by Jat and Chaudhury women and nangna by Gujjar women. [dabu:S6]

Sanganer syahi-begar designs were used for local men's safas, while buti florals were favoured by the Jaipur court. [sanganeri:S8, sanganeri:S9]

concepts.title: Bagru and Sanganeri: a shared process chain
concepts.summary: Both GI texts print ferrous syahi (usually with the outline block) and alum begar.
concepts.body_md:
Both GI texts print ferrous syahi (usually with the outline block) and alum begar. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Both obtain green by yellow-dyeing indigo-dyed cloth after re-printing dabu to keep some blue. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Four persons hold the cloth while a fifth rubs on turmeric-pomegranate dye with a loose woollen cloth. [bagru:S1, sanganeri:S1]

Bagru prints differ from Sanganeri mainly in the off-white versus white background. [bagru:S1, bagru:S4]

claims.text: Both GI texts print ferrous syahi (usually with the outline block) and alum begar.
Both obtain green by yellow-dyeing indigo-dyed cloth after re-printing dabu to keep some blue.
Four persons hold the cloth while a fifth rubs on turmeric-pomegranate dye with a loose woollen cloth.
Bagru prints differ from Sanganeri mainly in the off-white versus white background.

relationships.explanation: Both GI texts give the same recipe: black clay, lime, wheat flour and gum, in ratios set by the dabu type, with family-held recipes.
relationships.conditions: The Bagru and Sanganeri GI documents share near-identical wording, so this agreement is not independent corroboration. The Bagru paste concept is needs_evidence (conflicting meanings of bidhan).

relationships.explanation: Bagru dabu and Akola-centred Dabu sources both name black clay as the resist base, mixed with lime and gum.
relationships.conditions: Dabu sources also give riverbank mud and river-bed silt; which clay is used varies by centre.

relationships.explanation: Both are clay pastes bound with gum that resist indigo; Ajrakh adds millet flour, Dabu recipes add lime and wheat by-products.
relationships.conditions: Ajrakh gach is also an alum carrier (see the gach/dabu-printing contrast).

relationships.explanation: Ajrakh gach carries alum, so one printing both resists indigo and mordants the later red; Bagru dabu is a pure resist, used only to make patterns in indigo.
Both traditions use a lime-based resist for fine lines: Ajrakh khariyanu white outlines, and Dabu lime (kirana) as the weakest resist for fine outlines.
relationships.conditions: In Ajrakh the lime also discharges alum; no Dabu source records that effect.

relationships.explanation: Wet resist paste is dusted at once with sawdust (Ajrakh also cow dung or rice husk) to stop the clay smudging.
Both GI texts say sawdust absorbs water from the dabu and adds a further resist layer.
relationships.conditions: Shared GI wording; not independent.

relationships.explanation: Resist strength is chosen for the number of dye immersions it must survive: mud for repeated indigo dips (Dabu sources); kaligar, dolidar and gawarbali types at Bagru.
relationships.conditions: The Dabu concept is needs_evidence; both rest on medium/low sources.

relationships.explanation: Both record that mud resist gives imprecise lines: Sanganeri dabu gives no sharp definition because the paste is thick and sticky; Akola printers moved to tar for finer designs because mud cracked.
After indigo, the clay resist is washed off, leaving the reserved pattern.
relationships.conditions: Akola tar resist is boiled off instead of washed.

relationships.explanation: Wax resist (applied with a kalam and removed by boiling) contrasts with a clay paste that is block-printed and washed off.
relationships.conditions: The wax account is a general kalamkari description, not Pedana-specific; the Machilipatnam concept is needs_evidence.

relationships.explanation: Machilipatnam prints indigo directly in rice starch, since indigo needs no mordant; Dabu reserves areas with a resist and dips the whole cloth in a cold vat.
relationships.conditions: Other Machilipatnam sources describe wax-resist-and-dip indigo in general kalamkari; synthetic blue is reported to have replaced natural indigo there.

relationships.explanation: The dyer decides how many dips (and, in Ajrakh, re-prints of resist between dips) are needed for the shade.
Both are tacit judgements of vat condition without a written recipe; the cue differs: taste in Ajrakh accounts, vat colour at Bagru.
Once established, the vat is kept active for long periods by replenishing ingredients.
Identical descriptions: pleated cloth opened under the liquor, oxidised and re-dipped from pale sky blue to the desired shade.
relationships.conditions: Shared GI wording; not independent.

relationships.explanation: Both soak scoured cloth in myrobalan (harde/harda) solution and dry it as a tannin pre-mordant before mordant printing.
Both dip the scoured cloth in myrobalan and dry it, turning it yellowish before printing.
Identical peela karna: harda in water, submerge, squeeze, dry flat, fold and beat.
relationships.conditions: Shared GI wording; not independent.

relationships.explanation: Myrobalan soak, squeeze and dry, as the step before mordant printing.
Both are iron liquors from scrap iron fermented with jaggery, thickened or printed for black.
relationships.conditions: Recipes differ (gram flour and tamarind in Ajrakh; salt water and paddy husk at Machilipatnam).

relationships.explanation: Syahi in both is fermented iron (rusted horseshoes) with jaggery and gum that turns black with harda.
relationships.conditions: The GI texts share wording, but Sanganeri also has independent sources (Gaatha, Jain & Hada).

relationships.explanation: Both describe black made from iron (rust or filings) left with jaggery and water, printed as the black mordant.
relationships.conditions: Bagh sources also describe market-bought ferrous sulphate cooked with tamarind seed powder.

relationships.explanation: Both describe printed mordants reacting in one alizarin bath to give different colours on the same cloth.
Identical statement: the dye reacts with two mordants at two locations, giving red with alum and black with ferrous.
relationships.conditions: Shared GI wording; not independent.

relationships.explanation: Alum and iron printed in different areas yield red and black when the whole cloth is boiled in a red bath.
The Ajrakh GI text says kut develops its black on printing, as iron reacts with the tannin on harde-treated cloth; a Bagh source says the black forms when alizarin reacts with iron in the dye bath.
relationships.conditions: Unresolved chemistry: see shared.open_question.iron-anthraquinone-colour-chemistry. The Bagh concept is needs_evidence.

relationships.explanation: Both add a colourant to the colourless alum paste: a simple chemical colour at Bagh, a pinch of geru (red ochre) at Sanganer.
relationships.conditions: Only the Bagh source states the purpose (to let the printer see placement); the Sanganeri sources give the ingredient, not the reason.

relationships.explanation: Practitioners keep a known spoiler away from the alum red: lime (which discharges alum) in Ajrakh, iron (which darkens the colour) at Machilipatnam.
Both sources say stray iron darkens the colours: iron in Ajrakh water dulls and darkens the result; Machilipatnam printers avoid iron utensils with alum for the same reason.
A late alum bath fixes the applied yellow: at Machilipatnam excess yellow runs off and colours are fixed; at Bagru alum makes the fugitive turmeric-pomegranate yellow fast.
In both, synthetic alizarin has replaced madder as the red dye and still develops red on alum.
Both record an earlier root dye (aal at Bagh; chay and madder in the south) replaced by alizarin.
relationships.conditions: Bagh sources disagree on what "aal" alizarin comes from (open question in the Bagh file).

relationships.explanation: Akola Dabu replaced alizarin with naphthol printed and developed in red salt; Sanganer replaced madder with synthetic alizarin but kept the alum-mordant bath.
Both GI texts say dhawai flowers are boiled with alizarin to avoid patches and staining.
relationships.conditions: Shared GI wording; not independent.

relationships.explanation: A flower boiled with alizarin in the red bath; Bagh sources identify the bhatti flower as Woodfordia fruticosa.
relationships.conditions: The stated role differs (shine and fixing at Bagh, avoiding patches at Sanganer); the Bagh concept is needs_evidence because its identity and role are disputed.

relationships.explanation: Both add dried flowers to the red bath to keep colour from staining where it is not wanted.
relationships.conditions: Different plants are named (tamarisk in Ajrakh; Woodfordia at Bagru); the similarity is of function only.

relationships.explanation: A locally gathered plant is added to the alizarin boil as a fixer: gaja leaves at Machilipatnam, dhavda flowers at Bagh.
relationships.conditions: Bagh concept is needs_evidence.

relationships.explanation: The red bath is heated in large copper vessels over a wood fire, with cloth kept moving by sticks.
relationships.conditions: Machilipatnam sources disagree on copper versus iron vessels.

relationships.explanation: Both record a shift to synthetic dyes, with natural dyes kept for particular orders or markets.
relationships.conditions: Neither tradition has a reliable measured share.

relationships.explanation: Both record synthetic dyes adopted for cost, time or demand alongside natural dyeing.
After the red bath, cloth is treated with dung, spread on a river bed or bank in the sun and kept moist to whiten the ground.
relationships.conditions: Camel dung in Ajrakh, cow dung at Sanganer.

relationships.explanation: Both GI texts attribute the whitening to dung combined with sun (and moisture).
relationships.conditions: Applicant explanations without measurement; the Sanganeri concept and the shared sun-bleaching mechanism are needs_evidence.

relationships.explanation: Repeated wetting while the cloth dries in the sun near running water, after dyeing.
Bagru keeps an off-white (cream) ground; Sanganer restores a white ground by sun-bleaching.
relationships.conditions: Both statements come partly from GI texts that share wording.

relationships.explanation: The Machilipatnam account leaves unmordanted areas pinkish after the alizarin bath; Sanganer whitens them again.
Mordant-printed cloth rests before washing so the colour or mordant sets.
relationships.conditions: Durations differ: 8–15 days at Bagh, at least 3–4 days at Bagru.

relationships.explanation: Mordant-printed cloth is left to dry and cure before washing.
relationships.conditions: Durations differ: one to three days at Machilipatnam, at least 3–4 days at Sanganer.

relationships.explanation: Printed cloth is washed in flowing water to remove unfixed mordant and gum before the red bath. Both sources warn about faulty washing: permanent stains at Bagh, colour developing in unwanted areas at Machilipatnam.
Washing out excess mordant in running water before dyeing.
Repeated overnight soaking in an oil, alkali or salt, and dung mixture: castor oil, soda ash and camel dung (Ajrakh, 8–10 times); castor oil, rock salt and goat dung (Bagh, three times).
Grey cloth is soaked overnight in dung and water, then washed and spread in the sun.
relationships.conditions: The Machilipatnam district page describes alkaline boiling instead, as current practice.

relationships.explanation: Ajrakh sources report iron in the water as harmful (dull, dark prints and black spots); a Bagh source credits the river's iron content, with running water, for finer colours.
relationships.conditions: The Bagh claim is untested and its concept is needs_evidence; Bagh sources disagree on the mineral.

relationships.explanation: Both GI texts credit local river water with properties good for dyeing, without measurement.
relationships.conditions: Both concepts are needs_evidence.

relationships.explanation: Both attribute characteristic colours to local water (with soil, sun or plants), without chemical evidence.
relationships.conditions: Both concepts are needs_evidence.

relationships.explanation: Printing settled where suitable water was available: soft water in Kutch, the Bagh river at Bagh.

Practitioners attribute shade differences to the water used: a Khavda printer says weather and water made shades differ; a Bagh artisan says reds and greys fix poorly when washing is done at the Narmada.
The river that drew printers has dried: Dhamadka's by 1989; Bagru's Sanjaria now runs dry while printing continues.
relationships.conditions: Ajrakh printers later relocated after the 2001 earthquake; Bagru printers did not move.

relationships.explanation: The local river fails (several times a year at Bagh, now permanently at Bagru), affecting washing.
Falling water tables threaten production, and used water is now treated or recycled.
Printing effluent pollutes local water, and sources blame screen or chemical printing rather than hand-block work.
relationships.conditions: The Machilipatnam concept is needs_evidence (journalism only).

relationships.explanation: Chemical residues from printing pollute local groundwater.
Both trace Khatri printers from Sindh about four centuries ago.
relationships.conditions: Dates in both files are contested (open questions); the Ajrakh concept is needs_evidence.

relationships.explanation: Hereditary Chhipa printers in both, linked to Sant Namdev.
Both centres are worked by the Chhipa community.
relationships.conditions: One craft organisation credits Dabu to the Khatri community (Dabu open question).

relationships.explanation: Bagru Chhipa accounts trace migration within Rajasthan and descent from Saint Namdeo; Ajrakh Khatri accounts trace migration from Sindh.
relationships.conditions: Not a clean opposition: Bagh sources call Khatris chhipas, and Bagru and Sanganer respondents were mostly Khatri or Chhipa.

relationships.explanation: Blocks are carved by a separate group of turners, the Kharadis, from shisham, mango and teak.
relationships.conditions: Shared GI wording; not independent.

relationships.explanation: Distinct designs and palettes for distinct client communities.
Designs and garment formats tied to the wearer's community, including Jat women in both accounts.
Design and colour chosen by user group and occasion.
relationships.conditions: Sanganer also served the Jaipur court, unlike the folk clientele of Bagru.

relationships.explanation: Ajrakh achieves a two-sided cloth by printing the reverse separately with registration; the Sanganeri GI specifies a single-face print that shows almost as vividly on the underside.
Aakola Dabu is an unregistered application at Pre Examination; Kutch Ajrakh is registered.
A secondary source reports a GI date that the registry contradicts (Dabu "2023", Bagru "2024").
Secondary sources give several GI years that differ from the registry record.
Screen-printed imitations sold under the tradition's name are cited in both GI applications.
relationships.conditions: Shared GI wording; not independent.

relationships.explanation: Cheaper screen-printed work with chemical colours competes with block printing.
relationships.conditions: Machilipatnam concept is needs_evidence.
